newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Serb returnees in Bosnia barred by Croats - UNHCR.
newsitem.headline: Serb returnees in Bosnia barred by Croats - UNHCR.

text.p: About 250 Bosnian Serb civilians trying to visit their hometown of Drvar in western Bosnia at the weekend were kept out by Croats, the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said on Tuesday.

Ron Redmond, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, told a news briefing that the group, part of a growing number of Serbs seeking return under the Dayton peace accords, went to the town on Sunday but were halted at the outskirts.
"The incident is especially tragic since the Drvar group is one of the few voices in the (Serb) Republika Sprska pressing for the right of minorities to return to their homes," he said.

Before the 1992-95 Bosnian war, Drvar, which lies inside the Moslem-Croat Federation to the south of Serb-controlled Banja Luka, had a population of some 14,000, almost entirely Serb. Most of them now are in Banja Luka.

"This is yet another example of the intransigence of the local Croat authorities in Dvar. The UNHCR has tried for months to facilitate assessment visits by this group of displaced persons to their hometown," Redmond said.
"We have mediated about 30 requests, and all have been rejected."

He added that most of the problems in implementing the Dayton accords, which provided for people to return to their original homes if they wished, had involved Moslems or Croats seeking to go back into what now is the Republika Srpska.
The Serb authorities have made clear they prefer a clear ethnic division and have generally discouraged Serbs from trying to go back to their homes inside the Federation.

"But there are also Bosnian Serbs trying to return to their home areas, and they too are being blocked," Redmond said. added. Others were trying to go back to Bosansko Grahovo near Drvar, where most of the 7,000 pre-war population was Serb.
However, in the south of the country there were positive signs that Serbs seeking to return to their homes in Moslem- controlled east Mostar were making some progress.

Redmond said the Moslem authorities in the city, the western part of which is controlled by Croats, had received a delegation of Serb displaced people last week and agreed to launch a pilot project for some returning residents.

This would initially involve 100 families. The Serb delegation had returned to Belgrade, where most of the displaced now are living, and would draw up a list of 100 houses and the names of the people who would move to them.
